title: Computable reductions and the undecidability of first-order logic
summary: Translate decision problems by total computable maps, then use the finite Robinson axioms to prove that first-order validity and satisfiability are undecidable.
abstract: To show that a problem is undecidable, it often suffices to translate a known undecidable problem into it. A many-one reduction makes this precise: a terminating computation transforms inputs while preserving both yes and no answers. Every computably enumerable set reduces to the halting problem, so halting can serve as a common target for all such recognition problems. A different reduction translates theoremhood in Robinson arithmetic into first-order validity, meaning truth in every structure. This proves that validity in the arithmetic language is undecidable, although proof search can enumerate its valid sentences. Satisfiable sentences in that language cannot even be enumerated by a program.
